title: Second-derivative and higher-derivative tests
terms: second-derivative test; higher-derivative test; degenerate critical point; local maximum; local minimum.

exposition.text:

At a stationary point a, f (a) > 0 implies a strict local minimum and f (a) < 0 a strict local
maximum, assuming the usual local differentiability needed by the test. If the second derivative

is zero, the test is inconclusive. The functions x , −x , and x illustrate minimum, maximum,
and neither despite the same first two derivatives at zero.
More generally, suppose f is sufficiently differentiable near a, its derivatives of orders 1 through

m gives a minimum for positive coefficient and maximum for negative coefficient; odd m gives
neither. If every derivative vanishes, this finite-order test says nothing.

question.text:
(j)
Suppose f is six times continuously differentiable near zero, f (0) = 0 for 1 ≤ j ≤ 5, and
(6)
f (0) = −12. Which conclusion follows?
(A) Zero is a strict local minimum.
(B) Zero is a strict local maximum.
(C) Zero is an inflection point.
(D) f is constant near zero.
(E) No conclusion about extrema is possible.

solution.text:
6 6
Taylor’s local formula gives f(x) − f (0) = −12x /6! + o(x ), which is negative for all suffi-
ciently small nonzero x. The first nonzero order is even with negative coefficient.

For which real a is zero a strict local minimum of f (x) = ax + x ?
(A) a = 0 only (B) a > 0 (C) a < 0 (D) Every real a (E) a ≥ 0

solution.text:

If a > 0, the leading fourth-power term is positive; if a = 0, x > 0 away from zero. For
a < 0, the leading term is negative, producing a local maximum instead.
